paragraphs.heading: What a neutron is
paragraphs.text: A neutron is a particle with no electric charge, and it weighs slightly more than a proton. Neutrons sit in the nuclei of atoms, next to a similar number of protons. A neutron is not an elementary particle, though: each one is built from three quarks. The science that describes how neutrons behave and interact is nuclear physics.

paragraphs.heading: Isotopes and a name
paragraphs.text: Atoms of one element can hold different numbers of neutrons. When two atoms of the same element differ only in that count, they are called isotopes of each other. The name neutron joins a Latin root meaning neuter with the Greek ending -on, the same ending heard in electron and proton.

paragraphs.heading: Life outside the nucleus
paragraphs.text: A neutron set loose from a nucleus does not stay a neutron. On its own it breaks down into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, with an average lifetime of about 15 minutes. Nuclear fission and fusion release free neutrons in large numbers, and research reactors, neutron generators and spallation sources make them on purpose for irradiation and scattering experiments. Earth even has a small natural background of free neutrons, produced by cosmic rays and by elements in the crust that split on their own.

paragraphs.heading: A puzzle in the nucleus
paragraphs.text: In Rutherford's 1911 picture, the atom was a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus inside a far bigger cloud of negative electrons. In 1920 he proposed that the nucleus also held neutral particles, which he imagined as a proton and an electron bound together. Through the 1920s physicists assumed nuclei were made of protons plus 'nuclear electrons'. From 1928 it became clear that this idea clashed with the new quantum theory, and it also failed to match the spins seen in atoms and molecules.

paragraphs.heading: Chadwick finds it
paragraphs.text: In 1931 Walther Bothe and Herbert Becker aimed alpha particles from polonium at beryllium, boron or lithium and got an unusually penetrating radiation. An electric field did not bend it, so they took it for gamma rays. The next year Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie found that this radiation knocked very energetic protons out of paraffin. James Chadwick, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, doubted the gamma ray reading and showed the radiation was made of uncharged particles with about a proton's mass. That matched Rutherford's predicted neutron, and Chadwick won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

paragraphs.heading: The road to nuclear power
paragraphs.text: By 1934 Fermi was firing neutrons at heavier elements to make them radioactive. Late in 1938 Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann found that neutron bombardment could break uranium nuclei into lighter elements, a process called nuclear fission. Before World War II was over, that finding had led to both nuclear power and the atomic bomb. The neutron is essential to making nuclear power.

paragraphs.heading: Stars and safety
paragraphs.text: Neutrons matter far from Earth too. Inside stars they play a major part in building chemical elements, through fission, fusion and neutron capture. Massive stars that collapse can form neutron stars, made of neutrons packed as tightly as an atomic nucleus yet holding more mass than the Sun. Back on Earth, free neutrons do not ionize atoms directly but do cause ionizing radiation indirectly, so depending on the dose they can harm living things.
